name: 2 Samuel
v: Word reached Joab: "The king is weeping. He's in mourning for Absalom."
So the day's victory curdled into grief for the whole army, because the troops heard it said: "The king is broken over his son."
The men slipped back into the city that day like soldiers slinking home in shame after running from a battle.
The king had covered his face. He was crying out at full voice: "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab marched into the king's quarters and let him have it: "Today you've humiliated every man who saved your life — your sons, your daughters, your wives, your concubines.

You love the people who hate you and hate the people who love you. You've made it clear today: your commanders and soldiers mean nothing to you. I see now — if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you'd be content.

Get up. Go out there. Speak to your men. Encourage them. Because I swear by the LORD — if you don't go out, not one man will stay with you tonight. And that disaster will be worse than every disaster you've faced from your youth until now."

So the king got up and took his seat at the gate. Word spread through the ranks: "The king is sitting at the gate." And the whole army came and stood before him.

Meanwhile Israel had scattered — every man back to his tent.
Across all the tribes of Israel, people were arguing: "The king rescued us from our enemies. He saved us from the Philistines. And now he's fled the country because of Absalom.
And Absalom — the one we anointed to rule us — is dead in battle. So why is nobody saying anything about bringing the king back?"

King David sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: "Speak to the elders of Judah. Ask them: 'Why are you the last to bring the king home? The talk of all Israel has already reached the king at his residence.
You're my brothers. My own bone and flesh. Why are you the last to bring the king back?'
And tell Amasa: 'Aren't you my own flesh and blood? May God do worse than the worst to me if you don't become my permanent army commander in place of Joab.'"
He won over every man of Judah as if they were one heart. They sent word to the king: "Come back — you and all your men."
So the king started home. He reached the Jordan, and Judah came down to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across.
Shimei son of Gera — the Benjaminite from Bahurim — hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand Benjaminites came with him. Ziba, the steward of Saul's house, was there too, along with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king,

crossing back and forth to ferry the king's household across and do whatever he wanted.

Shimei son of Gera threw himself down before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan.
He said, "My lord, don't hold my guilt against me. Don't remember what your servant did wrong the day you left Jerusalem. Don't let the king carry that against me.
I know I sinned. So here I am — the first one from the entire house of Joseph to come down and meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah broke in: "Shouldn't Shimei be executed for this? He cursed the LORD's anointed!"
David said, "What business is this of yours, sons of Zeruiah? You're acting like my enemies today. Should anyone in Israel be put to death today? Don't I know I'm king over Israel again?"
Then the king said to Shimei, "You will not die." And he swore it to him.
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, came down to meet the king. He hadn't cared for his feet, trimmed his mustache, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came home in peace.
When he arrived from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king asked him, "Why didn't you come with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answered, "My lord the king — my servant betrayed me. I told him, 'Saddle a donkey for me so I can ride out with the king' — because I'm lame, you know.
But he slandered me to my lord the king. Still, my lord the king is like an angel of God. Do what seems right to you.
My father's entire house deserved nothing but death from my lord the king. Yet you set me at your own table. What right do I have to ask anything more of the king?"
The king said, "Why keep talking? I've decided: you and Ziba will split the estate."
Mephibosheth said, "Let him have all of it. My lord the king has come home in peace — that's enough for me."
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king to send him on his way.
Barzillai was very old — eighty years. He'd kept the king supplied while he stayed at Mahanaim, because he was a man of immense wealth.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me. I'll take care of you in Jerusalem at my side."
But Barzillai answered the king, "How many years do I have left, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king?

I'm eighty years old. Can I tell good from bad anymore? Can your servant taste what he eats and drinks? Can I still hear singers, men or women? Why should your servant be one more burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will just cross the Jordan with the king a short way. Why repay me with a reward like that?

Let your servant turn back so I can die in my own town near the graves of my father and mother. But here is Kimham, your servant — let him cross over with my lord the king. Do for him whatever seems good to you."
The king said, "Kimham will cross over with me. I'll do for him whatever pleases you. And anything you want from me, I'll do for you."
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Kimham crossed with him. All the troops of Judah escorted the king across, along with half the troops of Israel.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king and complained: "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away? Why did they bring the king and his household across the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"

The men of Judah shot back at the men of Israel: "Because the king is our close relative. Why are you so worked up over this? Have we eaten at the king's expense? Have we taken anything for ourselves?"

The men of Israel answered Judah: "We have ten shares in the king — and we have more claim to David than you do. So why have you despised us? Weren't we the first to talk about bringing our king back?"

But the men of Judah came back harder than the men of Israel.

com.d:
# 2 Samuel 19: The Weight of Victory and Mercy

The deepest struggle of David's heart in this chapter is learning that military victory over enemies pales compared to the pain of broken relationships with his own people. As David grieves Absalom's death following his successful defeat of the rebellion, he discovers that winning a battle can feel like losing everything.

When David's commanders confront him, they name something true: his excessive mourning is dishonoring those who risked their lives to save him. Yet their rebuke, however necessary, cannot touch the father's grief. This is the human reality of leadership—we must sometimes carry sorrows that others cannot fully understand, and we must sometimes set aside our personal anguish to serve those who depend on us. David rises and takes his place, not because his pain has vanished, but because love for his people calls him forward.

What unfolds next is a portrait of reconciliation as difficult and necessary work. David shows mercy to those who opposed him—to Shimei, who cursed him; to Mephibosheth, whose loyalty seemed questioned; to Barzillai, whose faithful friendship needs honoring. These gestures cost David something real. They require him to absorb hurt, to trust again, to rebuild trust in a fractured kingdom. This is grace in its most practical form: choosing relationship over revenge, choosing the hard work of restoration over the satisfaction of retribution.

For those of us who lead, parent, or simply live in community, David's costly mercy speaks deeply. Reconciliation is not a feeling that arrives first; it is an action we take even when grieving, even when mistrustful, even when we'd rather withdraw into our pain. The kingdom requires us to move toward the broken places with open hands.

Where in your own life might you need to make the harder choice—not victory, but reconciliation? What would it cost you?
com.s:
The nineteenth chapter of 2 Samuel narrates the complex aftermath of Absalom's rebellion, focusing on David's restoration to the throne and the political tensions that accompanied his return to Jerusalem. This material belongs to the Court History of David (2 Samuel 9–20), a remarkably candid ancient Near Eastern historiographical work that unflinchingly portrays the human dimensions of royal power. The chapter divides naturally into several episodes: Joab's harsh rebuke of the grieving king, David's journey back to Jerusalem, and his encounters with various figures whose loyalties had been tested during the rebellion.

The chapter opens with David's excessive mourning for Absalom, which Joab identifies as politically dangerous. The verb translated "to mourn" (אָבַל, *ʾābal*) appears repeatedly, emphasizing the intensity of David's grief that threatens to alienate his loyal troops. Joab's confrontation employs the striking accusation that David "loves those who hate him and hates those who love him" (v. 6), articulating the fundamental tension between David's private emotions and public responsibilities. The term "shame" (בּוֹשׁ, *bôš*) pervades Joab's speech, indicating the social dimension of honor that David's behavior has violated.

David's return necessitates political reconciliation with those who supported Absalom. His appeal to Judah through the priests and his appointment of Amasa—Absalom's general—as commander replacing Joab represents strategic maneuvering that would later prove fatal. The verb "to incline" (נָטָה, *nāṭâ*) in verse 14 describes David bending the hearts of Judah toward himself, employing language elsewhere used of divine action upon human hearts.

The encounters with Shimei, Mephibosheth, and Barzillai each explore themes of loyalty, deception, and reward. Scholars debate Mephibosheth's sincerity—was he genuinely betrayed by Ziba, or does his unkempt appearance represent calculated performance? David's ambiguous judgment dividing the property suggests either Solomonic wisdom or royal weariness.

The chapter concludes with escalating tension between Judah and Israel over proprietary claims to the king, foreshadowing the eventual division of the monarchy. This passage demonstrates how personal grief, political calculation, and tribal rivalry intersected in ways that shaped Israel's destiny for generations.
com.p:
This chapter unfolds approximately one thousand years before Christ, in the aftermath of Absalom's rebellion, as David prepares to return to Jerusalem following his son's death. We stand here in the era of the united monarchy, that brief golden age between the establishment of the Davidic throne and its eventual fracturing under Rehoboam. Within the grand arc of redemption, this moment belongs to the Kingdom epoch—that period when God's rule over His people found its earthly expression through anointed kings who foreshadowed the coming Messiah.

David's restoration to his throne pulses with typological significance. The weeping king who crossed the Jordan eastward in shame now returns westward in restored glory, and in this crossing we glimpse the pattern that will find its fulfillment in Christ—the rejected King who passes through death's Jordan only to return in triumph. David's journey back pictures what the prophets would later proclaim: the Messiah would be despised and rejected, yet ultimately enthroned over all. The people who had followed Absalom now cry out for David's return, confessing that he had delivered them from their enemies, a repentance that shadows Israel's future recognition of the One they pierced.

The chapter teems with reconciliation and judgment held in tension. Shimei, who cursed David during his flight, now prostrates himself seeking mercy—and David grants it, overruling Abishai's demand for death. Here the anointed king exercises the prerogative that belongs supremely to Christ: to show mercy where justice might destroy. Mephibosheth's vindication before David anticipates how the true Son of David will judge rightly between the faithful and the treacherous, between those who genuinely mourned his absence and those who sought advantage in his humiliation.

Yet the chapter closes with ominous strife between Judah and Israel, tribal jealousies that will eventually tear the kingdom apart. This foreshadows the partial, provisional nature of all earthly restorations. David's return brought peace, but not permanent peace. The fractures remained, awaiting a greater King whose kingdom would know no division.

The church lives in the already of Christ's victorious resurrection-crossing and the not-yet of His final return. Like Israel awaiting David at the Jordan, we cry, "Why do you delay bringing back our King?" The same mercy extended to rebels, the same vindication promised to the faithful, the same throne awaiting its rightful occupant—all find their consummation when He who is greater than David returns to reign forever.
